cards.title: Spotting real problems: Where every great venture begins
facts: Entrepreneurs do not start with products; they start with genuine human frustrations, inefficiencies, and unmet needs.
The best student inventions solve everyday frictions they experience firsthand in school, transit, or neighborhood life.
do: Keep a 'Bug List' notebook where you write down 3 things that annoyed or slowed people down each day
Listen carefully to customer complaints: 'I hate waiting in this queue' is a direct business opportunity
Observe how people create makeshift hacks to solve problems—that hack is your product prototype
dont: Never start building a gadget or software without verifying that real people actually suffer from that problem
Never fall in love with your solution before falling in love with the problem

myths.statement: Great business ideas come exclusively from sudden lightning bolts of genius inspiration.
myths.truth: Vast majority of successful ventures originate from disciplined observation of everyday frictions and inefficiencies.

quiz.q: What is the most effective starting point for creating a successful student enterprise?
options: Designing a flashy logo before anything else
Identifying an unsolved recurring frustration that people already complain about
Copying an American tech company blindly
Borrowing huge bank loans
quiz.explanation: Businesses exist to solve real problems. Without an authentic pain point, products have no willing buyers.

rubric.point: Interview 5 classmates and the librarian to pinpoint exact friction points in locating books
rubric.keys: interview students and librarian|pinpoint friction|listen to users

rubric.point: Document the recurring pain point in a problem log before jumping into complex coding
rubric.keys: document pain point|validate need before building

rubric.point: Observe what temporary hacks students currently use to find books

dangerous: build an expensive app without talking to anyone
ignore the issue as not my job
print random posters

cards.title: Brainstorming without judgment: Divergent thinking
facts: Effective ideation has two distinct phases: Divergent thinking (generating wild quantity) and Convergent thinking (filtering feasibility).
Critiquing ideas early kills psychological safety and stops bold breakthroughs from ever surfacing.
do: Set a timer for 10 minutes and aim for at least 30 diverse ideas without evaluating any of them
Encourage wild, unconventional ideas—it is easier to tame a wild idea than invigorate a boring one
Build upon teammates' concepts using the phrase 'Yes, and...' rather than 'No, but...'
dont: Never ridicule a teammate's wild suggestion during the initial ideation phase
Never allow one dominant voice to monopolize the brainstorming whiteboard

myths.statement: In a brainstorming session, you should immediately reject impossible or absurd ideas as soon as they are mentioned.
myths.truth: Judging too early kills creative momentum. Absurd ideas often spark practical, revolutionary hybrid solutions.

quiz.q: Which conversational phrase encourages creative team ideation best?
options: 'That will never work'
'That sounds too expensive'
'Yes, and we could also add...'
'Our competitors already do that'
quiz.explanation: 'Yes, and...' accepts the premise and builds upon it, fostering psychological safety and compounding creativity.

situations: During an innovation club session at {at}, a quiet team member suggests using origami paper folding to package eco-friendly seed balls, but another student laughs.
scenario.question: How should {name} facilitate the team dynamic?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Remind the team that early brainstorming strictly suspends criticism to foster novel concepts
Build on the idea with 'Yes, and we can test recycled newspaper instead of fresh paper'
Ensure everyone gets uninterrupted turns to pitch their ideas onto the board

dangerous: join in mocking the unconventional idea
shut down the session in anger
let only the loudest student speak

cards.title: The builder trifecta: Hacker, Hustler, and Designer
facts: Enduring projects need diverse skill sets: the Builder (technical/craft), the Hustler (business/sales), and the Designer (user experience/storyteller).
Teams composed of clones with identical skills frequently fight over identical tasks and neglect essential sales and aesthetics.
do: Map each team member's natural strengths rather than assigning roles by friend popularity
Define clear owners for key pillars: Product Quality, Customer Outreach, and Visual Identity
Establish a weekly standup meeting where everyone answers: What did I do? What is next? Am I blocked?
dont: Never form a team where everyone wants to code or craft but no one wants to talk to customers
Never leave responsibilities ambiguous so tasks fall through the cracks

myths.statement: The best venture teams are formed by three best friends who all share the exact same strengths and hobbies.
myths.truth: Homogeneous teams leave massive blind spots in marketing, finance, or design. Complementary diversity drives success.

quiz.q: In classic venture building, what is the primary responsibility of the 'Hustler' role?
options: Writing backend server code
Talking to customers, securing sales, partnerships, and managing money
Drawing vector logo art
Cleaning the office floor
quiz.explanation: The hustler drives customer acquisition, communication, resource management, and commercial sustainability.

situations: At the science fair team registration at {at}, four friends all want to design the robotic arm, but no one wants to prepare the presentation deck or speak to judges.
scenario.question: How should {name} guide the team allocation?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Identify individual complementary strengths across building, communication, and visual design
rubric.note: Allocates roles based on functional diversity.

rubric.point: Assign a dedicated communicator/hustler responsible for judge presentations and user testing
rubric.note: Ensures vital outreach is not neglected.

rubric.point: Establish clear shared accountability and celebrate all roles equally

dangerous: let all four fight over the same robotic motor
force one person to do everything alone
quit the competition

cards.title: The 60-second elevator pitch: Hook, problem, solution, ask
facts: An elevator pitch summarizes your venture in under a minute: Hook, Problem, Solution, Traction/Secret Sauce, and the Ask.
If you cannot explain your project clearly in 60 seconds to a 10-year-old, you do not understand it well enough.
do: Structure your pitch: 'We help [Target User] solve [Urgent Problem] through [Unique Solution]'
Hook the listener in the first 10 seconds with a striking fact or relatable scenario
End with a concrete 'Ask' (e.g., 'We are looking for 10 beta testers' or 'Rs 500 seed material')
dont: Never recite complex technical jargon or buzzwords that confuse listeners
Never exceed your time limit during school pitch competitions

myths.statement: An elevator pitch should cram in every single technical line of code and feature specification.
myths.truth: Pitches are designed to spark curiosity and secure a follow-up conversation, not deliver an exhaustive user manual.

quiz.q: What are the four essential building blocks of a concise 60-second pitch?
options: Logo, office address, favorite color, price tag
Hook, Problem, Solution, and Clear Ask
Technical dictionary, apologies, long backstory, resume
Jokes, complaints, excuses, phone number
quiz.explanation: Hook catches attention, Problem establishes urgency, Solution shows value, and the Ask specifies next steps.

scenario.question: How should {name} structure the presentation?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Open with a sharp hook on students losing phone battery during emergency commutes

Conclude with a clear ask for student testers to trial the prototype next week

dangerous: ramble about solar physics for 55 seconds without stating what the product is
exceed time limit
read monotonously from paper

cards.title: Running a school carnival stall: Unit economics and cash floats
facts: A successful retail stall requires knowing your Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), setting a profitable price, and keeping an exact cash float for change.
Revenue is not profit; if you make Rs 2,000 in sales but spent Rs 1,800 on ingredients, your actual profit is only Rs 200.
do: Calculate unit cost: total ingredient/material expense divided by number of servings produced
Price items to cover costs plus a 30-50% profit margin while remaining affordable for students
Prepare a cash box with plenty of Rs 10, Rs 20, and Rs 50 notes and coins for customer change
dont: Never consume stall food or give freebies to friends without accounting for them in the ledger
Never leave the stall cash box unattended at any time

myths.statement: If your stall collects Rs 3,000 cash in the cash box at the end of the day, your team has earned Rs 3,000 profit.
myths.truth: Gross sales revenue must subtract material costs, stall entry fees, and packaging before net profit is known.

quiz.q: If you spend Rs 300 to make 30 bookmarks and sell all 30 at Rs 20 each, what is your net profit?
options: Rs 600
Rs 300 (Rs 600 revenue minus Rs 300 cost)
Rs 20
quiz.explanation: Net Profit = Total Revenue (30 x 20 = Rs 600) minus Total Cost (Rs 300) = Rs 300.

situations: {name}'s student club at {at} prepares homemade lemonade for the annual sports day carnival.
scenario.question: How should {name} manage the stall's financial operations?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Tally all expenses for lemons, sugar, cups, and ice to calculate exact unit cost per cup
rubric.note: Establishes accurate cost of goods sold.

rubric.point: Maintain an organized cash box with small change and record every sale in a ledger
rubric.note: Ensures cash flow integrity and customer service.

rubric.point: Calculate net profit only after fully reimbursing initial material costs
rubric.keys: net profit after costs|reimburse seed money

dangerous: eat stock without paying
leave cash box open on table
assume all revenue is pure profit

cards.title: Embracing failure: 'No' is just data, not defeat
facts: Every renowned entrepreneur faced dozens of rejections before finding product-market fit; rejection is simply market feedback.
Treating failure as learning (iteration) separates enduring creators from those who give up at the first hurdle.
do: When someone says 'No thanks', ask politely: 'Could you share what you would change about this?'
Keep an 'Iteration Log' tracking what worked, what flopped, and what adjustment to test next
Separate your personal self-worth from your product prototype; your idea was rejected, not you
dont: Never take constructive customer feedback as a personal insult or attack
Never repeat the exact same flawed pitch without modifying your approach

myths.statement: If the first five customers you approach reject your product, you should immediately quit entrepreneurship.
myths.truth: Early rejection is standard. World-class founders test hundreds of iterations based on early critique before finding traction.

quiz.q: What is the most constructive response when a customer declines to buy your homemade product?
options: Argue with them angrily
Politely ask what feature or pricing would make it genuinely useful to them
Cry in the hallway
Lower the price to zero
quiz.explanation: Customer objections provide the exact roadmap needed to refine product features and value.

situations: At the craft fair at {at}, {name}'s hand-painted clay pots receive zero purchases in the first three hours while visitors walk past.
scenario.question: How should {name} respond constructively?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Step out and politely ask browsing visitors what designs or products they were hoping to find
rubric.keys: ask visitors feedback|listen to objections|market discovery

rubric.point: Notice that visitors are asking for functional drainage holes or smaller desk sizes
Pivot the display and signage to highlight practical desk utility rather than giving up

dangerous: pack up and leave in despair
insult customers for having poor taste
slash prices below material costs

cards.title: The Mom Test: Gathering genuinely honest customer feedback
facts: Asking 'Do you like my idea?' prompts friends and family to lie politely to avoid hurting your feelings.
The famous 'Mom Test' rule: Ask about their past behaviors, real habits, and actual money spent, never theoretical opinions.
do: Ask: 'How do you currently handle this problem?' rather than 'Would you buy my app?'
Look for evidence of action: If they haven't spent time or money trying to fix it, the problem isn't urgent
Listen 80% of the time and speak only 20% during user research interviews
dont: Never ask leading questions like 'Don't you think my handmade badge is awesome?'
Never count polite compliments from best friends as proof of market demand

myths.statement: Asking your parents and best friends 'Would you buy this?' gives completely reliable market validation.
myths.truth: Loved ones lie to encourage you. Only observed actions, past spending, and neutral feedback reveal true demand.

quiz.q: Which interview question provides the most honest validation about a new study-planner tool?
options: 'Don't you think my study planner is pretty?'
'How did you organize your exam revision last week, and what frustrated you about it?'
'Will you promise to buy this when it launches?'
'Do you love apps?'
quiz.explanation: Asking about specific past behavior uncovers actual user friction without fishing for polite compliments.

situations: {name} develops a prototype cardboard desk organizer at {at}. Friends say 'It's super cool!' but no one asks to keep one.
scenario.question: How should {name} validate true user demand?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Apply the Mom Test: observe whether students actually put pens into it and ask what they currently use
rubric.keys: apply mom test|observe real usage|probe past habits

rubric.point: Avoid relying on polite verbal compliments as proof of commercial viability
Ask students what specific desk clutter problem frustrates them most during homework

dangerous: assume instant success based on friend compliments
force friends to buy out of obligation
stop asking questions

cards.title: Milestones & Gantt charts: Turning chaotic projects into reality
facts: Ambitious ventures collapse when teams wait until the final 48 hours to assemble prototypes and posters.
Backward planning (working back from launch day) breaks daunting projects into bite-sized weekly milestones.
do: Pinpoint launch day and work backwards: prototype ready by Day 10, testing by Day 15, launch by Day 20
Assign a single accountable owner and deadline for every sub-task on a shared visual checklist
Hold a 5-minute daily check-in to identify blockers before they cause multi-day delays
dont: Never leave deadlines as 'sometime next week' without an exact day and time
Never let silent bottlenecks fester without asking team members for help

myths.statement: Leaving all project tasks open-ended without deadlines sparks spontaneous creative genius.
myths.truth: Unstructured timelines breed chronic procrastination and emergency all-nighters that destroy build quality.

quiz.q: What is the core principle of 'backward planning' for a school project exhibition?
options: Starting on the first day and improvising as you go
Setting the final exhibition date as the target and scheduling reverse deadlines for each milestone
Doing all the work the night before
Waiting for teachers to assign dates
quiz.explanation: Reverse scheduling ensures every necessary phase—sourcing, fabrication, testing, and rehearsal—has dedicated time.

situations: With a science-venture exhibition only 3 weeks away at {at}, {name}'s team has many ambitious ideas but zero physical prototypes built.
scenario.question: How should {name} structure the project timeline?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Create a backward schedule: Week 1 prototype build, Week 2 user testing, Week 3 presentation rehearsal
Assign specific component ownership (hardware, poster, script) with hard Friday check-ins
Identify critical dependencies early so delay in sourcing does not stall the entire team

dangerous: wait until day 20 to start assembling parts
blame teammates without setting deadlines
abandon the project

cards.title: Sweat equity vs shortcuts: Real enterprise takes patience
facts: Social media glamorizes teenage dropouts making millions overnight through dropshipping or crypto; real enterprise is built on patient iteration.
Sustainable businesses require deep craftsmanship, customer empathy, ethical supplier relationships, and operational discipline.
do: Focus on mastering a craft or solving a tangible community need rather than pursuing overnight viral wealth
Celebrate small milestones: your first paying non-family customer is worth more than 10,000 viral views
Be suspicious of any course, influencer, or book promising guaranteed passive income with zero effort
dont: Never sacrifice product quality, safety, or ethical honesty to make a quick buck
Never jump between five unrelated business ideas every two weeks without executing one thoroughly

myths.statement: Successful entrepreneurs achieve wealth effortlessly within a few weeks using automated internet shortcuts.
myths.truth: Enduring businesses require years of hard work, continuous iteration, and solving complex real-world challenges.

quiz.q: Which mindset is essential for enduring entrepreneurial success?
options: Hunting for overnight get-rich-quick hacks
Patient craftsmanship, resilience through setbacks, and genuine customer focus
Copying someone else's viral video
Avoiding hard work at all costs
quiz.explanation: Real value creation requires continuous learning, resilience, and ethical problem solving over long horizons.

scenario.question: How should {name} evaluate this proposition?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Reject the get-rich-quick shortcut, recognizing that sustainable ventures solve real human needs
rubric.note: Rebuffs speculative traps in favor of genuine value.

rubric.point: Continue iterating the recycling initiative through measured customer feedback
Evaluate business ideas based on tangible utility rather than flashy influencer hype

dangerous: gamble project funds on trading bots
quit school to pursue viral fame
believe automated riches hype

cards.title: Servant leadership: Lead by clearing obstacles, not giving orders
facts: Being the project leader does not make you a royal monarch; effective leadership means serving your team and clearing their roadblocks.
Dictatorial leaders alienate talented peers, while empathetic servant leaders inspire voluntary excellence and shared pride.
do: Ask teammates daily: 'What is blocking you, and how can I help you finish it?'
Publicly credit teammates for successes while personally absorbing blame for collective mistakes
Do the unglamorous grunt work (cleaning up tools, organizing files) alongside your team
dont: Never micromanage competent teammates or bark orders like an autocrat
Never steal credit for a teammate's creative design during showcase presentations

myths.statement: A strong team leader should make every single minor decision alone and command teammates without discussion.
myths.truth: Command-and-control alienates team members. Great leaders empower peers, delegate trust, and facilitate consensus.

quiz.q: What is the hallmark behavior of a true 'servant leader' on a student project?
options: Ordering everyone around with a megaphone
Asking how to clear roadblocks for teammates and sharing credit generously
Taking all the praise on stage
Leaving early while others clean up
quiz.explanation: Servant leaders view their job as supporting and empowering their team to do their best work.

scenario.question: How should {name} exercise constructive leadership?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Facilitate a calm discussion focusing on objective design criteria rather than personal egos

rubric.point: Help test both bracket options experimentally to let data decide the better solution

rubric.point: Acknowledge both teammates' creative efforts and keep the team atmosphere supportive
rubric.note: Maintains high team morale and unity.

dangerous: scream at both members to obey captain orders
kick both members off the team
flip a coin without testing

cards.title: Honest marketing: Communicating value without exaggeration
facts: Great marketing connects a real solution with the people who need it; deceptive advertising destroys trust permanently.
Clean visual hierarchy (Headline, Benefit, Proof, Call to Action) outperforms cluttered, exaggerated promotional posters.
do: Follow the rule of three: Highlight 1 big headline, 3 key benefits, and 1 clear next action
Use high-contrast colors and legible fonts that can be read from 5 meters away
State exactly what your product can and cannot do with absolute honesty
dont: Never make false medical, environmental, or performance claims on your promotional flyers
Never use stolen copyrighted logos or watermarked images without attribution

myths.statement: Marketing means exaggerating your product's capabilities as much as possible so customers buy it.
myths.truth: Exaggeration creates disappointed customers who demand refunds and destroy your reputation. Honest marketing builds loyalty.

quiz.q: Which element makes a promotional event poster most effective at school?
options: Ten different fancy cursive fonts with glitter text
A bold readable headline, clear user benefit, event time/venue, and simple contact info
Twenty paragraphs of fine print
Stock photos of celebrities without permission
quiz.explanation: Clear visual hierarchy and legible essential facts inform viewers quickly and drive action.

scenario.question: How should {name} refine the marketing message?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Replace misleading hyperbole with honest value: 'Fast brake tune-ups, tire checks, and chain lubrication by students'
rubric.keys: honest value proposition|replace hyperbole|clear service list

rubric.point: Ensure the poster features clear dates, room location, and pricing or free-service details
Use clean visual layout with plenty of white space so key information stands out

leave off location and time
copy commercial brand logos

cards.title: Upcycling ventures: Turning discarded waste into community wealth
facts: Waste-to-wealth enterprises apply circular economy principles, transforming discarded trash (paper, fabric scraps, plastic) into valuable products.
Circular ventures generate revenue while reducing municipal landfill pollution, creating dual economic and ecological impact.
do: Identify clean waste streams available in large quantities (e.g., used exam notebooks, textile scraps from tailors)
Design an upcycled product that people want for its quality, not just out of sympathy for the environment
Calculate production costs thoroughly to ensure the recycled item is economically viable
dont: Never produce flimsy novelty items that break immediately and end up back in the landfill in 24 hours
Never collect hazardous or medical waste for school recycling projects

myths.statement: Eco-friendly upcycled products will sell automatically even if the build quality is poor and pricing is double market rate.
myths.truth: Eco-friendly benefits cannot compensate for terrible utility. Sustainable products must deliver equal or superior quality and fair pricing.

quiz.q: What is the core principle of a 'circular economy' venture?
options: Throwing away goods after a single use
Designing systems where materials are reclaimed, upcycled, and kept in productive use continuously
Burning plastic waste in open fields
Mining more raw metals from nature
quiz.explanation: Circular models minimize waste by cycling existing materials through reuse, remanufacture, and upcycling.

make unusable shoddy notebooks and force teachers to buy
discard clean paper

cards.title: Social enterprise: Doing good by doing sustainable business
facts: A social enterprise uses commercial market strategies to solve social, cultural, or environmental problems self-sustainably.
Unlike traditional charities reliant on perpetual donations, a social enterprise earns revenue from sales to fund its community mission.
do: Identify a clear double bottom line: Financial sustainability AND measurable social or environmental impact
Ensure the business model generates sufficient gross margin to survive without continuous grant dependency
Engage the beneficiary community as partners and co-creators rather than passive charity recipients
dont: Never treat social enterprise as an excuse for sloppy accounting or poor product standards
Never prioritize short-term profit at the cost of the core social mission

myths.statement: Social enterprises are identical to standard charities and cannot charge money for their products or services.
myths.truth: Social enterprises sell products or services commercially to generate independent revenue that perpetually powers their social mission.

quiz.q: What defines the 'double bottom line' of an authentic social enterprise?
options: Earning twice as much personal money as traditional jobs
Measuring both commercial financial sustainability AND positive social/environmental impact
Filing two sets of tax returns
Operating in two different countries simultaneously
quiz.explanation: A double bottom line holds the enterprise accountable to financial health and measurable positive community impact.

rubric.point: Reinvest platform profits into potter apprenticeships and clay sourcing infrastructure

exploit artisans for personal profit

cards.title: Approaching mentors: Specific questions and respecting time
facts: Experienced professionals love helping proactive, respectful young builders who demonstrate initiative and do their homework.
Vague requests like 'Can you be my mentor?' get ignored; concise, specific questions about a concrete challenge get enthusiastic replies.
do: Research the mentor's past work before reaching out so you can reference specific relevant projects
Ask 1 or 2 focused questions that can be answered in under 5 minutes or a brief 15-minute call
Always send a follow-up thank-you note sharing what action you took based on their advice
dont: NEVER send a generic 'Hi sir, please mentor me' message without context or proof of work
NEVER expect busy mentors to do your homework, write your business plan, or review 40-page decks

myths.statement: Busy industry professionals never respond to student emails or messages.
myths.truth: Most leaders gladly help passionate students who write concise, polite, well-researched emails showing genuine commitment.

quiz.q: What is the most effective way to request guidance from an experienced entrepreneur?
options: Send a 20-page business proposal with no introduction
Send a polite 4-sentence email introducing your project, asking one specific question, and offering flexible 15-minute time slots
Call their personal phone repeatedly during dinner hours
Ask them to fund your entire project upfront
quiz.explanation: Concise, specific emails that respect the recipient's schedule have the highest response rates.

rubric.point: Ask one precise technical question regarding laser sensor baseline calibration in dusty weather
rubric.note: Respects their time with a focused inquiry.

rubric.point: Keep the message under 150 words and express gratitude for their published research papers

demand immediate video calls
copy-paste generic spam template

cards.title: Win-win negotiation: Getting what you need while helping others
facts: Negotiation is not a combat sport where one party crushes the other; enduring business relationships require both sides to win.
Focus on interests, not rigid positions: understanding what the other party truly values unlocks creative compromises.
do: Understand the other party's constraints (e.g., a vendor may lack cash but have surplus warehouse space)
Identify non-monetary trade-offs: publicity, volunteer labor, flexible delivery dates, or barter exchanges
Know your BATNA (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement) before starting any discussion
dont: Never use aggressive ultimatums or threats during business or school negotiations
Never agree to a deal that leaves you harboring deep resentment or severe financial loss

myths.statement: In a good negotiation, you must trick or force the other party into losing as much as possible.
myths.truth: Win-lose deals cause the loser to sabotage delivery, breach contracts, or refuse future collaboration. Win-win builds enduring partnerships.

quiz.q: What does the term 'BATNA' mean in negotiation strategy?
options: Buying All The New Assets
Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement (your backup plan if talks fail)
Borrowing All Total Net Amounts
Billing Always Takes New Accounts
quiz.explanation: Your BATNA is your walk-away alternative; knowing it gives you confidence to negotiate calmly without desperation.

rubric.keys: free seats for staff children|shared value

abandon the workshop without discussion
break into the hall secretly

cards.title: Balancing grades and building: The Eisenhower Matrix
facts: Student builders who neglect board exam studies fail school; student builders who never execute remain dreamers.
The Eisenhower Matrix categorizes tasks into four quadrants: Urgent & Important, Important but Not Urgent, Urgent but Not Important, and Neither.
do: Schedule 90-minute deep work blocks for school revision before opening project software
Spend time daily in Quadrant 2 (Important, Not Urgent: strategic building, health, revision) before crises hit
Say 'no' to time-wasting social obligations and mindless scrolling that drain builder energy
dont: Never sacrifice 7+ hours of essential nightly sleep to crunch on startup prototypes
Never use your venture as a psychological excuse to evade fundamental homework commitments

myths.statement: Real founders sleep only 3 hours a night and completely fail their high school classes to succeed.
myths.truth: Sleep deprivation destroys cognitive performance and decision making. High achievers master focused time blocking.

quiz.q: According to the Eisenhower Matrix, which quadrant should ambitious student builders prioritize to prevent perpetual crises?
options: Quadrant 4 (Mindless video games and gossip)
Quadrant 2 (Important but Not Urgent: planning, proactive study, prototype testing)
Quadrant 3 (Every random notification that rings)
Quadrant 1 (Only emergency fire-fighting)
quiz.explanation: Investing focused time into Quadrant 2 prevents tasks from exploding into stressful last-minute emergencies.

cards.title: Street-smart economics: Lessons from chaiwallas and kirana stores
facts: Local street vendors, chaiwallas, and kirana shopkeepers are master entrepreneurs in cash flow, inventory turnover, and customer loyalty.
Silicon Valley buzzwords often obscure fundamental retail truths that local bazaar merchants execute flawlessly every single day.
do: Observe how chai vendors manage zero-waste just-in-time inventory with perishable milk and tea leaves
Study how neighborhood kirana owners remember customer family names and personalize credit to build unbreakable loyalty
Notice prime foot-traffic location dynamics: why a vendor sets up right beside a bustling railway exit
dont: Never dismiss humble informal merchants as uneducated; their practical business mastery is formidable
Never overlook unit economics and daily cash reconciliation in favor of abstract software theories

myths.statement: You can only learn valid business strategy from billionaires and professors at elite business schools.
myths.truth: Informal street merchants possess deep mastery of micro-location, rapid inventory turns, customer psychology, and cash resilience.

quiz.q: What critical business lesson does a busy morning chaiwalla demonstrate perfectly?
options: Carrying massive 3-year stockpiles of milk
High-speed execution, minimal inventory holding cost, and unbeatable customer relationship warmth
Spending millions on billboard advertising
Ignoring customer preference
quiz.explanation: Street vendors excel at high-velocity turnover, zero dead stock, tight working capital, and personal rapport.

scenario.question: What entrepreneurial insight can {name} extract from this observation?
scenario.bubble: What is the safest move right now?

rubric.point: Recognize active inventory preservation (damp sacks protect perishables) and merchandising (eye-level display)
rubric.note: Extracts practical supply chain and retail principles.

rubric.point: Appreciate how daily customer relationship trust enables small businesses to thrive without advertising budgets
rubric.note: Values customer loyalty and retention dynamics.

rubric.point: Document practical operational lessons in a personal business observation notebook
rubric.note: Translates everyday observation into actionable insights.

dangerous: mock street vendors as unsophisticated
assume only app startups have valid business models
ignore real-world commerce

cards.title: Intellectual property & plagiarism: Building on original work
facts: Copying someone else's logo, design, or written code and calling it your own is intellectual theft and copyright infringement.
Ethical builders leverage open-source licenses, attribute original creators properly, and focus on adding genuine novel value.
do: Check open-source license terms (MIT, Apache, Creative Commons) before using third-party code or media
Always provide clear attribution to original creators when remixing public domain resources
Protect your own original designs by documenting creation dates and applying for school innovation patents where appropriate
dont: NEVER copy a competitor's logo, trademark name, or marketing slogans for your project
NEVER submit someone else's project work into a science competition as your own

myths.statement: If an image or code snippet is visible on Google, it is free for anyone to use commercially without permission or credit.
myths.truth: Publicly visible does not mean copyright-free. Most web content is protected by automatic copyright requiring explicit licensing.

quiz.q: What is the required practice when using an open-source icon pack or software library in your student project?
options: Claim that you designed all the icons from scratch in Photoshop
Check the license terms (e.g., Creative Commons / MIT) and include required creator attribution
Remove the copyright notices from the code files
Sell the icon library to classmates
quiz.explanation: Open-source licenses require honoring attribution terms and keeping licensing notices intact.

Include a dedicated credits section acknowledging open-source tools and fonts used in the project

lie to competition judges about origin
